subject: English
name: English, Year 9
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: English, Level 9

points.title: Language that builds rapport
points.brief: Inclusive pronouns such as we and us, shared jokes, a friendly tone and showing agreement draw a speaker and audience closer.

points.title: Allusion
points.brief: An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known person, story or event, which brings its meaning into the text without explaining it.

points.title: Evocative vocabulary
points.brief: Words chosen to call up strong feelings and pictures, such as shattered rather than broken, reveal the writer's view and stir the reader's.

points.title: Adapting a text structure
points.brief: Writers bend a usual structure for a purpose, such as an argument told as a story or a report told as a list, to surprise or engage readers.

points.title: Condensing information with noun groups
points.brief: Long noun groups and nominalised words pack a lot of information into few words, as in the rapid growth of online shopping.

points.title: Reference words and cohesion
points.brief: Words such as this, these, such and the former point back to earlier ideas, linking sentences without repeating them.

points.title: Abstract nouns that summarise
points.brief: An abstract noun such as this injustice or the decision can sum up a whole idea from an earlier sentence and carry it forward.

points.title: Sentence fragments for effect
points.brief: A sentence fragment lacks a main clause but can be used on purpose for emphasis or shock, as long as the writer controls it.

points.title: Varying sentence length
points.brief: Mixing short and long sentences, and starting them in different ways, keeps writing lively and lets the most important point stand out.

points.title: Word choice and mood
points.brief: The vocabulary a writer chooses builds the mood of a passage, such as gloomy, peaceful or tense, and shapes the writer's style.

points.title: Quotation marks, ellipses and square brackets
points.brief: Quotation marks show exact words, an ellipsis shows words left out, and square brackets show words added to make a quotation fit.

points.title: Citing sources
points.brief: Naming the author, title and date of a source, in the text and in a reference list, gives credit and lets readers check it.

chapters.title: Symbols, light and sound on screen

points.title: Visual symbols
points.brief: Objects and colours in images can stand for ideas, such as a wilting flower for loss or red for danger or passion.

points.title: Lighting and colour in film
points.brief: Bright, even lighting feels safe and open, while dim lighting with strong shadows creates mystery or threat.

points.title: Soundtrack and silence
points.brief: A soundtrack can signal how to feel, and a sudden silence can make a moment shocking or tense.

points.title: Stereotypes and complex characters
points.brief: A stereotype reduces a group to a few fixed traits, while a complex character has mixed qualities and can change, which makes a representation fairer.

points.title: Representations of place by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors often represent places as Country, with deep connections to people, culture and history.

points.title: How responses change on rereading
points.brief: A first reading gives an impression, and later readings notice more detail and patterns, which can change or deepen a personal response.

points.title: Moral positions in literature
points.brief: Literary devices and images can lead readers to judge a character's choices as right or wrong, and to accept or question the text's values.

points.title: Extended metaphor
points.brief: An extended metaphor carries one comparison through several lines or a whole text, such as life described as a journey.

points.title: Metonymy
points.brief: Metonymy names something by a thing closely linked to it, such as the crown for a king or queen, or the press for journalists.

points.title: Allegory
points.brief: An allegory is a story whose characters and events stand for ideas or real events, so it carries a second, hidden meaning.

points.title: Symbolism in literature
points.brief: A symbol is an object, character or setting that stands for something larger, often appearing again at important moments.

points.title: Aesthetic qualities
points.brief: Aesthetic qualities are what make a text striking or beautiful to read, such as its rhythm, imagery and shape, and how they add to meaning.

points.title: Verse novels and graphic novels
points.brief: Hybrid forms mix features, such as a verse novel telling a story in poems or a graphic novel telling it through panels, words and images.

points.title: The unreliable narrator
points.brief: An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted, because they lie, misunderstand or leave things out, so readers must look past what they say.

points.title: Non-linear structures
points.brief: Starting in the middle of the action, ending where the story began, or jumping between times changes how readers piece the story together.

points.title: Rhetorical devices in speeches
points.brief: Speakers use groups of three, repetition at the start of lines, contrast and direct address to make ideas memorable to listeners.

points.title: How a text positions its audience
points.brief: Through what it shows first, whose voice it gives and its word choice, a text leads its audience towards a particular response.

points.title: Representations of concepts over time
points.brief: Ideas such as heroism, family or success are represented differently in different times and cultures, which shows a text's context.

chapters.title: Spelling and voice on the page

points.title: Non-standard spelling for effect
points.brief: Writers may spell words as they are spoken, or break spelling rules, to create humour, a character's voice or a distinctive style.

points.title: Writing accents and dialects
points.brief: Spelling and grammar can be changed on the page to show how a character speaks, which should be done with care so it is not a mockery.

points.title: Spelling plurals
points.brief: Common plural patterns such as adding -es after s, x or ch, changing y to ies, and f to ves, and plurals that change completely.

points.title: Explicit values in language
points.brief: Writers state their beliefs and attitudes outright through judging words, strong claims and direct calls for action.

points.title: Organising ideas in paragraphs
points.brief: Each paragraph develops one idea from a topic sentence, and the order of paragraphs builds an argument or story towards its point.

points.title: Comparing texts
points.brief: Comparing two texts means finding what they share and how they differ in ideas, purpose and techniques, then explaining why.

points.title: Contention and supporting arguments
points.brief: A contention is the main point a writer argues, and each supporting argument gives a reason with evidence for it.

points.title: Rebuttal
points.brief: A rebuttal states an opposing argument and shows why it is weak, which makes the writer's own case stronger.

points.title: Editing paragraphs for control
points.brief: Editing checks that each paragraph has one clear focus, sentences are varied and correct, and the vocabulary is precise.
